title: Optimal In-context Adaptivity and Distributional Robustness of Transformers
claim: In-context learning handles tasks of differing difficulty: the same prompt-to-output format yields simple answers on easy tasks and harder ones on difficult tasks.
layout: 2-column by 2-row table, top-to-bottom prompt then output, color-coded text

In the easy column these are Genetics → Biology and Relativity → Physics, followed by a red query 'Topology → ?'. In the difficult column these are Cat → 10, Fish → 25, Deer → 17 and Dog → 13, followed by a red query 'Bird → ?'. The bottom row, labeled 'Output', gives the green answers: 'Mathematics' for the easy task and '9' for the difficult task. Color encodes role: blue for examples, red for queries, green for outputs. Black table lines separate the cells. The eye goes first to the colored arrow lists.
caption: Two ICL tasks. Blue indicates the (in- context) examples, red indicates the queries, and green indicates the outputs.
abstract: We study in-context learning problems where a Transformer is pretrained on tasks drawn from a mixture distribution $Ï=\sum_{Î±\in\mathcal{A}} Î»_Î± Ï_Î±$, called the pretraining prior, in which each mixture component $Ï_Î±$ is a distribution on tasks of a specific difficulty level indexed by $Î±$. Our goal is to understand the performance of the pretrained Transformer when evaluated on a different test distribution $Î¼$, consisting of tasks of fixed difficulty $Î²\in\mathcal{A}$, and with potential distribution shift relative to $Ï_Î²$, subject to the chi-squared divergence $Ï^2(Î¼,Ï_Î²)$ being at most $Îº$. In particular, we consider nonparametric regression problems with random smoothness, and multi-index models with both random smoothness and random effective dimension. We prove that a large Transformer pretrained on sufficient data achieves the optimal rate of convergence corresponding to the difficulty level $Î²$, uniformly over test distributions $Î¼$ in the chi-squared divergence ball. Thus, the pretrained Transformer is able to achieve faster rates of convergence on easier tasks and is robust to distribution shift at test time. Finally, we prove that even if an estimator had access to the test distribution $Î¼$, the convergence rate of its expected risk over $Î¼$ could not be faster than that of our pretrained Transformers, thereby providing a more appropriate optimality guarantee than minimax lower bounds.
